title: CAP, PACELC & Consistency Models
summary: The theory that frames every distributed database trade-off — what CAP actually forces you to choose, the latency half PACELC adds, and the spectrum of consistency guarantees between strict correctness and raw speed.

slides.markdown:
Every distributed database eventually has to answer: when a network hiccup splits your cluster in two, do you keep serving requests (and risk giving different answers on each side) or refuse to answer at all until the split heals? That's the choice the **CAP theorem** forces, and it's the single most-quoted — and most-misunderstood — idea in distributed systems interviews.

This topic covers what CAP actually proves (and the common misreading of it), **PACELC**'s extension to the latency trade-off that exists even without a partition, and the practical spectrum of consistency models — strong, eventual, causal, and tunable — that real databases let you choose per operation, not just once at the whole-system level.

The **CAP theorem** says a distributed data system can provide at most two of three properties **simultaneously during a network partition**: **Consistency** (every read sees the most recent write, or an error), **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps working despite dropped or delayed messages between nodes).

The part interviewers actually want you to know: partition tolerance isn't optional in a real distributed system — networks *will* partition, whether from a switch failure, a cross-region link dropping, or just packet loss. So the real choice CAP forces is between **C and A when a partition happens**, not a free pick of any two of three at all times.

When there's no partition, a well-built system can be both consistent and available — CAP only bites during the partition itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the choice during a partition (CP vs AP)
slides.markdown:
![CP refuses the client's write during a partition while AP accepts it and risks disagreement](assets/cp-vs-ap-partition.svg)

During the partition, the left side has exactly two options for the client's request: refuse it (protecting consistency, sacrificing availability — **CP**) or accept it and risk disagreeing with the right side once the network heals (protecting availability, sacrificing consistency — **AP**).

There's no third option that gives both during the partition itself — that's the whole content of the theorem.

assets.alt: CP refuses the client's write during a partition while AP accepts it and risks disagreement

slides.sectionTitle: PACELC: the else-latency half people forget
slides.markdown:
CAP only describes behavior **during a partition (P)** — but partitions are rare; most of the time your system is running normally, and CAP says nothing about that case. **PACELC** fills the gap: *if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.*

The "else" half matters because it applies during normal, everyday operation, not just rare partition events: a system that wants strong consistency has to coordinate across nodes (wait for a quorum, or route to a single leader) on every operation, which costs latency, even when the network is perfectly healthy. A system willing to accept slightly stale reads can skip that coordination and respond faster.

This is why PACELC is considered the more complete framework in practice — CAP only tells you what happens on a bad day, PACELC also tells you what you're paying on every normal day.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: strong vs eventual vs causal consistency
slides.markdown:
| | Strong | Eventual | Causal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guarantee | Every read sees the latest write, everywhere | Reads eventually converge, no ordering promise in the meantime | Causally related writes are seen in order; unrelated ones may not be |
| Latency cost | Highest — needs coordination per operation | Lowest — no coordination needed | Moderate — tracks causal dependencies, not full ordering |
| Example | Bank balance after a transfer | Follower counts on social media | A comment shown only after the post it replies to |
| Typical systems | Single-leader relational DBs (reads from leader) | DynamoDB, Cassandra (default) | Version-vector or session-based systems |

**How to decide:** ask whether the application can tolerate a stale read at all (strong), can tolerate it as long as related events stay in order (causal), or genuinely doesn't care as long as it converges eventually (eventual).

slides.sectionTitle: Tunable consistency: quorum reads and writes
slides.markdown:
Rather than picking one consistency level for an entire system, many databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak) let you tune it **per operation** using the quorum parameters introduced in Replication: with `N` replicas, a write succeeds after `W` acknowledge it, and a read queries `R` replicas and reconciles.

Setting `W = N` and `R = 1` gives fast reads but slow, less available writes (every replica must confirm). Setting `W = 1` and `R = N` gives fast, available writes but slow reads. Setting `R + W > N` (e.g. `N=3, W=2, R=2`) is the common middle ground — it guarantees every read overlaps with the latest acknowledged write, giving you strong-ish consistency without requiring every single node to participate in every operation.

The key insight: consistency isn't binary in these systems — it's a knob you can set differently for a user's profile read (fine with eventual) versus their account balance read (wants the quorum guarantee).

**Wrong belief:** "We want a CA system — consistent and available, no partition tolerance needed, since our network is reliable."

**Why it's wrong:** this treats partition tolerance as an optional feature you can opt out of, like a checkbox. In reality, any system with more than one node connected by a real network *will* experience partitions eventually — a switch fails, a cable gets cut, a cloud region has a networking incident. "No partition tolerance" doesn't mean partitions won't happen; it means the system has no defined, safe behavior for when they do, which usually means silent data corruption or an outage worse than a clean CP/AP trade-off would have produced.

**Correct model:** partition tolerance isn't a choice, it's a fact of distributed systems. The actual engineering decision is what happens during that inevitable partition — reject requests (CP) or risk divergence (AP) — and that choice can even vary by operation within the same system (strongly consistent for payments, available-first for a "like" counter).

slides.sectionTitle: Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and other client-facing guarantees
slides.markdown:
Beyond the big three (strong/eventual/causal), production systems often promise narrower, cheaper guarantees that solve specific user-facing complaints without paying for full strong consistency everywhere.

**Read-your-writes**: a user always sees their own writes, even if others might not yet (solves the "my comment disappeared" bug from Replication). **Monotonic reads**: once a client has seen a value, it never sees an older one on a later read — without this, a user could refresh a page and watch a counter go backward as their request happens to hit a less-caught-up replica. **Monotonic writes**: writes from one client are applied in the order that client issued them, even under replication.

These session-level guarantees are usually implemented by routing a client to a consistent replica, or by having the client carry a version token forward — much cheaper than making the whole system strongly consistent for everyone.

slides.sectionTitle: Real systems on the CAP spectrum
slides.markdown:
Naming real systems against the theory is what separates a memorized definition from applied understanding. **Single-leader relational databases** (Postgres, MySQL reading from the leader) behave **CP**: during a partition that isolates the leader, they refuse writes rather than risk two leaders diverging. **DynamoDB and Cassandra default to AP**: during a partition, both sides keep accepting writes and reconcile later — that's the whole reason quorum tuning exists, to let you dial consistency back up per-operation when you need it. **ZooKeeper and etcd are deliberately CP**: they exist specifically to be a trusted source of truth (leader election, config), so they refuse to serve if they can't guarantee correctness, by design.

The practical lesson: "CP vs AP" isn't a database's permanent personality — it's a design decision the vendor made, often exposed as a config knob you can retune for your workload.

slides.sectionTitle: PACELC in numbers: the latency you're actually paying
slides.markdown:
The "else-latency" trade-off is easy to underrate until you see numbers. A single-region quorum write with `W=2` of `N=3` typically adds low **single-digit milliseconds** over a same-datacenter network — cheap. The same quorum spanning **three regions** (say us-east, eu-west, ap-south) can push write latency to **150–300ms**, because the write has to wait for acknowledgment from at least one far-away replica.

This is precisely why globally distributed systems (Cassandra multi-region, DynamoDB Global Tables, CockroachDB) often default to weaker per-region consistency with async cross-region replication — paying milliseconds of eventual staleness cross-region is usually a better trade than paying hundreds of milliseconds of latency on every single write.

Interview signal: connecting PACELC's "latency" half to a concrete cross-region millisecond figure — not just naming the acronym — is what shows you've actually reasoned about the trade-off.

slides.sectionTitle: Staff-level nuance: consistency as a per-operation decision
slides.markdown:
A junior answer picks one consistency model for "the database." A staff-level answer recognizes that a real production system almost never needs uniform consistency everywhere — and forcing it either wastes latency budget or risks correctness where it matters.

Concretely: an e-commerce platform might use strong consistency (or a full ACID transaction) for **inventory decrement at checkout** — overselling is a real cost — while using eventual consistency for the **"customers also viewed"** recommendation widget, where a few seconds of staleness is invisible to the user and free in latency terms. Both live in the same system, often the same database, tuned per query or per table.

The interview-differentiating move is naming *which specific operations* need which guarantee and why, rather than declaring the whole system "eventually consistent" or "strongly consistent" as a single label — that framing itself is usually the tell of a shallower answer.
